Early Layer Sensitivity for Subgroup
Audit Prioritisation with GradientGuard
DIDULA FERNANDO and MANINDA EDIRISOORIY A
ABSTRACT Early model measurements may help allocate limited inspection effort to classiﬁers that
later exhibit subgroup failures despite healthy source performance. We investigate layer-wise connection
sensitivity as an additional signal for this decision. GradientGuard summarises the distribution of
absolute weight–mean-gradient products across shallow and deep network blocks during the ﬁrst ten
percent of training. A staged investigation combines analytical implementation checks, saved-checkpoint
probe-partition analysis, a completed outcome experiment with 96 classiﬁers in 24 conﬁguration
families, and post-hoc diagnostics of frozen forecasts. The source-normal held-out cohort contains
36 classiﬁers and 12 terminal worst-group failures. Six non-slope layer summaries increase average
precision from 0.775 to 0.934 and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.816
to 0.962 relative to the selected conventional predictor. At twelve inspections, both six- and eight-
feature layer variants discover ten failures, compared with eight for conventional and global-sensitivity
predictors; this pattern persists across the two probe-panel variants examined. At the original nine-
inspection endpoint, all four predictors discover eight failures. Whole-family uncertainty includes zero
improvement, and one inﬂuential-family omission reverses the larger-capacity comparison. The two
added layer-share slopes reach the estimator but add no discovery beneﬁt to the six-feature variant
in the primary cohort. These results identify non-slope layer summaries as a promising candidate for
independent validation while bounding current claims to an exploratory, benchmark-speciﬁc association.
INDEX TERMS Audit prioritisation, connection sensitivity, early training, subgroup robustness, worst-
group accuracy.
I. INTRODUCTION
A
GGREGA TE accuracy can conceal large differences
between subpopulations. A classiﬁer that performs
well on common combinations of object and background
may still fail on less common combinations, making source
performance alone an incomplete guide to robustness [ 1]–
[3]. When many candidate models are being trained, a
developer may have capacity to investigate only a subset in
detail. This creates a model-level decision: which apparently
healthy runs should receive a later subgroup audit?
We study whether the allocation of early connection
sensitivity across network layers provides additional infor-
mation for that decision. For a frozen model, connection
sensitivity is the absolute product of a learned weight and
its mean data-loss gradient. Its mathematical primitive is
established in pruning and zero-cost model assessment [ 4],
[5]. A global total records the magnitude of this sensitivity;
a normalised layer proﬁle records where it is allocated.
These quantities can differ even when model outputs and
total weight sensitivity agree. This distinction motivates a
predictive experiment, rather than demonstrating that layer
proﬁles encode subgroup reliance.
The operational research question is: Among classiﬁers
that appear healthy early in training, does the allocation of
connection sensitivity across layers improve prioritisation
for terminal subgroup-failure audits beyond conventional
telemetry, global sensitivity and matched layer-wise struc-
tural statistics? In simple terms, we ask whether knowing
where a model’s loss is sensitive helps choose which models
to inspect. This is local sensitivity to multiplicative weight
changes on a speciﬁed source probe, not a causal account
of visual feature reliance. “Hidden” refers to unavailable
terminal group outcomes at the early decision point; audit
groups are predeﬁned.
This article reports a completed exploratory investigation.
A measurement-feasibility study established numerical cor-
rectness and useful between-run level variation. A targeted
follow-up examined probe partitions, classiﬁer-head aggre-

II. RELATED WORK AND INFORMATION BOUNDARIES
A. PREDICTION FROM EARL Y TRAINING INFORMATION
Naik et al. [6] use early loss, accuracy, gradient signal-
to-noise, weight-norm growth, activation saturation and
hyperparameters to predict training outcomes. This estab-
lishes a substantial conventional-information baseline for
any proposed internal feature. Monin [ 7] studies prospec-
tive prediction of persistent out-of-distribution degradation
from source-side dynamics. The latter’s event-conditioned
trajectory setting differs from a single ﬁxed early prediction
of a completed classiﬁer’s subgroup-audit outcome, but
changing the target alone does not establish methodological
originality.
SPARE [ 2] identiﬁes early output structure associated
with spurious correlations and uses importance sampling
for mitigation. Our bounded class-conditioned probability-
clustering comparator adapts a discovery signal to model-
level forecasting; it does not reproduce SPARE’s complete
algorithm. In particular, this proof of concept uses probabil-
ity vectors, whereas the relevant published experiments also
use logit-based signals. Prediction depth [ 8] is another useful
comparator, but is not implemented here. Accordingly, we
do not claim improvement beyond prediction depth or
beyond a full reproduction of these prior systems.
B. SENSITIVITY AND LA YER STATISTICS
SNIP [4] supplies the connection-sensitivity primitive. Zero-
cost proxies [ 5] already aggregate related scores for eventual
model-performance ranking. SSNR/T-CET [ 9] explicitly
studies saliency composition and layer-aware aggregation,
while ZiCo [ 10] uses gradient-variation information. Early
sensitivity and the observation that aggregation can discard
layer information therefore have clear prior art.
Weight-distribution statistics also predict network accu-
racy [ 11]. Bohadana, Schneider and Katz [ 12] investigate
performance prediction using weights and gradients; this
is especially close technical prior art for internal layer
histories. Our literature audit distinguishes the accepted
publication record from the accessible associated manuscript
version. The present experiment does not implement that full
temporal predictor or the richer matched marginal-statistic
controls subsequently proposed. Its result is therefore an in-
crement over the implemented conventional/global controls,
with sensitivity-speciﬁc originality still to be established.
C. AUDITING AND GENERALISATION MEASURES
Subgroup discovery and model selection use information
regimes different from ours. Domino [ 13] identiﬁes system-
atic error slices, and SubpopBench [ 3] highlights ordinary
worst-class information as a relevant robustness signal. Our
early features use ordinary source labels; group annotations
are required for historical terminal outcome labels and
later evaluation. The system neither discovers arbitrary new
groups nor eliminates the need for group-labelled audits.
Studies of generalisation measures [ 14], [ 15] motivate
preserving conﬁguration structure instead of interpreting
pooled correlations as universal mechanisms. In our design,
the splitting and uncertainty unit is the setting family.
Different random seeds within a family, alternative probe
panels and overlapping capacity points are not independent
experimental settings. These distinctions are central to in-
terpreting the positive signals reported below.
D. THE PRECISE GAP AND CANDIDATE
CONTRIBUTION
The distinguishing question is conditional and decision-
speciﬁc: does a small allocation representation improve
the ranking of source-normal completed runs after the
information already supplied by ordinary training teleme-

proposing another saliency formula. The derivative, normal-
isation and descriptive summaries are inherited operations;
the candidate methodological contribution is their ﬁxed,
low-dimensional use in a carefully separated model-audit
forecasting task.

B. ARCHITECTURE AND ALLOCATION
CNN A has three 3 × 3 padded convolutions with widths
3 → 16 → 32 → 64, trainable biases and rectiﬁed linear
activations. The ﬁrst two stages have 2 × 2 max pooling.
Global average pooling feeds a biased 64 → 10 classiﬁer.
There is no batch normalisation or dropout. The shallow
block contains conv1 kernels; middle contains conv2 ker-
nels; deep combines conv3 kernels and classiﬁer weights.
Individual learned-layer totals and bias diagnostics remain
available.

For the same eligible candidate pool of N classiﬁers, rank
frozen failure probabilities in descending order, breaking
ties by run identiﬁer. Inspect k = ⌊0.25N ⌋ in the original
primary experiment. Let F be the observed number of
failures and DA(k) the failures discovered by predictor A.
Report precision DA/k, recall DA/F , random expected

B. SOURCE CONSTRUCTION AND RESERVATIONS
The outcome study uses ofﬁcial SpuCoMNIST with one
class per digit and RGB 28 × 28 inputs [ 16]. Its
24 setting families are the Cartesian product of align-
ment probabilities 0.10, 0.50, 0.80, 0.95, background dif-
ﬁculties MAGNITUDE_LARGE/MAGNITUDE_MEDIUM
and Adam learning rates 0.0003, 0.001, 0.003. Alignment
denotes the fraction assigned the class-associated colour;
ten-colour independence corresponds to 0.10, not zero.
The ﬁxed palette, digit identities, ordinary labels and no-
noise/no-augmentation choices are veriﬁed. Inspection of
the pinned generator established that LARGE modiﬁes zero-
background pixels over the image, while MEDIUM uses a
4×4 corner mask. The ofﬁcial implementation was checked
for all 48 seeded source constructions; foreground pixels
and labels were preserved. Each construction has 48,004
source-training identities: 256/class are reserved for panel
A, another 256/class for B and 128/class for source health,
leaving 41,604 training examples. Reservations use ordinary
class labels only, with disjoint original MNIST identities and
ofﬂine background metadata.
Each family has two source constructions and two ini-
tialisations per construction. Its four classiﬁers remain to-
gether through splitting, cross-validation and resampling. A
conﬁguration-only split with ﬁxed seed 81001 allocates 14
families/56 runs to development and ten families/40 runs
to evaluation, with every factor level represented on both
sides. These are 24 setting families sharing MNIST, not 96
independent benchmark draws.
C. TRAINING AND TERMINAL OUTCOMES
All models train from scratch with Adam betas (0.9, 0.999),
no weight decay, batch size 128, no dropped ﬁnal batch
and a constant learning rate. There are 326 updates per
epoch, including a ﬁnal four-example batch. The frozen full
horizon is 60 epochs or 19,560 updates. Early observation
steps are 196, 391, 587, 978, 1467, 1956, corresponding to
rounded 1%, 2%, 3%, 5%, 7.5% and 10% fractions. Every
non-diverged scientiﬁc model completes the full horizon; all
96 did so.
Source-normal eligibility is measured independently at
10% on the health panel: accuracy at least 0.80, mean cross-
entropy at most ln(10) and ﬁnite required measurements.
Ineligible models remain in the full-cohort analysis. The
secondary 5% predictions retain the same 10%-deﬁned
cohort rather than selecting a new favourable population.
Development terminal labels use ofﬁcial validation iden-
tities, evaluation labels ofﬁcial test identities. A common
outcome panel per difﬁculty/split uses ﬁxed approximately
balanced class/background assignments. Each model has
100 predeﬁned digit/background groups, with observed
group sizes 89–135. Deﬁne WGA = min g cg/ng and failure
as WGA < 0.75; equality is non-failure. We retain group
counts and marginal 95% Wilson diagnostics. These are not
simultaneous uncertainty bounds for the minimum. Fixed
0.70/0.80 sensitivity cutoffs and continuous worst-group
regression are secondary. Missing groups, numerical fail-
ures and incompleteness are separate statuses, not silently
converted to subgroup failures.

E. OUTCOME BOUNDARY AND ROBUSTNESS
ANAL YSIS
Design and family manifests precede collection. Develop-
ment classiﬁers and validation outcomes precede predictor
ﬁtting. Saved pipelines, inputs and hyperparameters are
frozen before held-out early risks; those risks are frozen
before test outcomes are unsealed. The saved audit veriﬁes
this order and the hashes. The 21 outcome integration
checks and complete-horizon audit support implementation
correctness, not predictive superiority.
Panel A is primary. Secondary checks apply frozen A
pipelines to panel B and use previously ﬁtted B pipelines
with A-selected choices. The post-hoc study loads these ex-
isting variants without reﬁtting. It computes every capacity
k = 0, . . . , N and marks nine/twelve inspections; twelve is
one third for the source-normal pool and 30% for the full
pool.
Uncertainty uses 2,000 paired draws of all ten held-
out setting families, seed 130005, keeping nested runs
together and recomputing pool size, ranking and fractional
capacity. The historical empty/single-outcome exclusion
rule is retained for interval comparability: 1,942 draws
are valid and 58 invalid. Raw discovery counts remain
deﬁned for single-outcome pools. Percentile intervals are
conditional on frozen forecasters and observed outcomes,
exclude forecaster-selection uncertainty, and are pointwise
rather than simultaneous evidence across a searched capacity
curve.
Leave-one-family-out analysis removes each of the ten
families, including the one with no eligible models. Frac-
tions 1/4 and 1/3 are recomputed using the remaining
pool. A family omission is an inﬂuence diagnostic, not an
independent replication. The post-hoc stage reproduces 27
saved-prediction comparisons to maximum absolute error
approximately 1.11×10−16 and passes 16 diagnostic checks.

C. PRIMARY CAP ACITY AND RANKING METRICS
At the original nine-audit capacity, E, B, L2, L6 and L8 each
ﬁnd eight of twelve failures (Table 5). Precision is 0.889,
recall 0.667 and random expected discoveries three. This
is useful prioritisation relative to random selection for the
measured pool, shared by the methods; it is not incremental
discovery evidence for GradientGuard.
The secondary ranking improvement is appreciable. L6
increases average precision from 0.7751 to 0.9336 and
receiver-operating-characteristic area from 0.8160 to 0.9618
relative to E, with a lower Brier score. L8 has the same
reported ranking metrics and a slightly lower Brier score
than L6. These observations motivate studying layer end-
point/mean/spread information, while the shared-bias con-
trol’s strong ranking metrics also motivate richer structural
comparisons.
The primary oracle ceiling is nine, leaving E only one
additional possible discovery. Its maximum ∆20 is therefore
20/36 ≈ 0.556, below the prospective useful-gain target of
one. This limited headroom explains why that target was
unattainable in the realised pool at nine audits; it does not
convert the observed tie into success.

F . WHAT THE SLOPES CONTRIBUTED
Both layer-share slopes survive imputation, scaling and
constant-feature ﬁltering. They have genuine variation and
enter L8. The shallow and deep standardised coefﬁcients are
approximately 0.01175 and −0.00444, with mean absolute
logit contributions 0.00618 and 0.00313. Their small effects
in this ﬁtted model cannot be attributed to accidental feature
omission.
L6 and L8 probabilities are not identical: the maximum
absolute difference is 0.002954, and four rank positions
differ. Their label order nevertheless produces the same
average precision, receiver-operating-characteristic area and
entire primary discovery curve. The selected audit sets are
identical at nine inspections; at twelve they overlap in
eleven of twelve candidates while retaining the same ten
discoveries. Equal ranking metrics do not establish identical
complete rankings.
Frozen-input replacement further localises the effect. Re-
placing one or both slopes by saved development-training
reference means sets their standardised components to zero
without ﬁtting. The largest probability change is 0.004761
for shallow replacement, 0.002062 for deep replacement and
0.006829 for both. The logit identity holds within about
6.11 × 10−16. No primary-cohort discovery count changes
at any budget. This can create unusual feature combinations
and is not a causal intervention or a retrained slope-free
model. Together with the predeﬁned L6 ablation, it supports
prioritising non-slope summaries for a fresh test rather than
asserting directional-slope value.

256/class budget, none of 96 runs crosses the descriptive
head-at-least-50%-of-deep or bias-at-least-10%-of-weight-

VI. COMPUTATIONAL COST AND REPRODUCIBILITY
The outcome archive records 94.14 minutes of classiﬁer
training, 5.20 minutes of six-checkpoint panel-A monitor-
ing, 5.29 additional minutes for panel B, 5.10 seconds
of early health assessment and 1.93 minutes of initializa-
tion monitoring. Summed classiﬁer invocation wall time
is 109.72 minutes. The panel-A path includes ordinary
telemetry and clustering as well as sensitivity, so its cost
is not an isolated incremental price for GradientGuard. The
second panel is research-validation overhead rather than a
production requirement.
The largest recorded allocated GPU-memory counter is
567.2 MiB. It is cumulative per process and does not
isolate incremental probe memory, other GPU applications
or CPU peak memory. Compact source data occupy 57.6
MiB and classiﬁer artifacts 110.3 MiB. Dataset preparation,
terminal evaluation and forecaster ﬁtting were not separately
instrumented; precise end-to-end component claims would
require improved logging.
The numerical stack is Python 3.12.14, PyTorch
2.7.1+cu128, torchvision 0.22.1+cu128 and CUDA runtime
12.8 on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti. Training uses
ﬂoat32, deterministic operations and no mixed precision or
reduced-precision shortcuts. Exact package records, seeds,
pinned SpuCo source hashes, conﬁguration snapshots and
failed engineering attempts are retained. The later diagnostic
environment repair restored a matching interpreter path
without changing the 80 dependency records. Reproducibil-
ity is conditional on compatible hardware/software, not
guaranteed across arbitrary systems [ 17].
The public repository [ 18] contains source, conﬁgura-
tions, compact identity manifests, ﬁgures, tables, reports,
decisions and frozen forecaster artifacts. Environments, raw
benchmark downloads, generated numerical dataset arrays
and classiﬁer weight/recovery ﬁles remain local; a clone
therefore requires reconstruction rather than claiming to
include every binary. Historical scientiﬁc ﬁles were imported
without line-ending conversion. The manuscript’s evidence
manifest records the exact archived ﬁles used for its tables
and ﬁgures.
VII. DISCUSSION AND SCOPE OF THE FINDINGS
The encouraging result is concentrated and interpretable:
non-slope layer summaries improve secondary ranking mea-
sures and yield more discoveries at several capacities in
a source-normal benchmark cohort. Panel-B checks retain
the twelve-audit pattern, and the full curve reveals useful
ranking structure beyond a single selected point. These
observations justify testing the narrower representation with
independent conﬁguration families.
The directional interpretation is different. The eight-
feature method was the prospective primary candidate, but
its two extra slopes contribute no discovery gain over L6 in

of a training preﬁx; the present ﬁndings do not establish that
endpoint proﬁles alone sufﬁce, or that all temporal informa-
tion is unhelpful. The L2–L6 ranking difference motivates

Sensitivity-speciﬁc originality also remains a testable
hypothesis. Existing work already uses early telemetry,
weights, gradients, saliency totals and layer-aware aggre-
gation. A rich control incorporating ordinary layer norms,
parameter/gradient marginals and shared bias diagnostics
could explain the observed L6 beneﬁt. A matched control

Table 8 distinguishes what the archive establishes from
the next study’s hypotheses. L6 is a prospective focus
selected by this exploratory evidence; the table does not
reclassify it as the original primary method.
The main statistical constraint is family diversity. The
held-out source-normal set has only three failure-bearing
families and no mixed-outcome family. Shared MNIST and
outcome panels add dependence beyond repeated seeds. The
bootstrap describes a small frozen-predictor setting mixture,
and the inﬂuential-family reversal prevents interpreting the
two-discovery point estimate as a reliable generalisation im-
provement. The intended primary generalisation is ranking
models from previously unseen setting families within the
studied benchmark, not necessarily distinguishing initiali-
sation seeds within one setting. Homogeneous outcomes
within each eligible family prevent assessing the latter,
but do not by themselves invalidate the former. A future
design should seek adequate development outcome support
and precision before spending its ﬁnal evaluation budget,
without replacing unfavourable families or tuning cutoffs
after outcomes. Mixed-outcome families are informative
diagnostics, not a requirement imposed retrospectively on
every setting.
The practical interpretation is similarly conditional. At
the same number of audits the methods spend the same
audit capacity; an increased yield is not automatically a
monetary saving. Inexpensive benchmark group evaluation
may favour auditing every classiﬁer. A realistic use case
requires a costly audit or an early reservation deadline,
plus monitoring overhead that is justiﬁed by the value of
additional discoveries. This study demonstrates a ranking
decision and observation timing, not operational deployment
savings.
The revised proposal describes stronger global and struc-
tural controls and a separately designed Waterbirds repli-
cation. These remain prospective. No Waterbirds results,
pretrained-model transfer evidence, fresh 256-run validation
or new forecaster ﬁtting are presented here. The initial
nonlinear comparator’s small-fold splitting limitation, the
bounded probability-based SPARE adaptation and omitted
prediction depth further bound claims against strong al-
ternatives. Completing those checks would strengthen the
next test, while a result explained by simpler layer statistics
would support a narrower contribution.
A. A BOUNDED VALIDATION CONTRACT FOR THE
REVISED CLAIM
The existing results select a research hypothesis, not a
new primary result on the consumed test set. The next
study should designate L6 prospectively and compare three
ordered claims: added audit yield beyond conventional
telemetry, beyond a strong global-sensitivity predictor, and
a conditional increment beyond a rich structural bank. The
matched structural pair must use the same development-
selected bank, cohort, folds, preprocessing and learner class,
adding only Z to the second input set with comparable
hyperparameter allowance. Different ﬁtted regularisation is
reported as part of the learning procedure, rather than
interpreted as an isolated feature intervention.
The decisive speciﬁcity comparison is a strong con-
ventional/global/structural predictor versus that same in-
put bank augmented with exactly the six L6 shares. The
structural bank should include layer weight/gradient norms
and their products, distribution statistics for parameters and
mean-probe gradients, and shared bias diagnostics. Separate
competing feature banks are useful ablations, but cannot
substitute for this nested pair. These measurements can be
validated using existing checkpoints as engineering ﬁxtures;
ﬁtting or selecting against their already known held-out
labels would remain exploratory. A claimed sensitivity-
speciﬁc advance requires fresh evaluation of the ﬁxed pair.
This comparison directly tests the alternative explanation
identiﬁed by both reviewers and the literature audit.
Both benchmark protocols, family allocation, eligibility,
failure cutoff, audit capacity, estimand and decision rules
must precede new evaluation outcomes. The proposed one-
third capacity is motivated by consumed diagnostics and
must be disclosed as such. The original nine-audit tie
remains unchanged. The proposed second-context Water-
birds experiment would use its own development/evaluation
separation; it cannot become independent conﬁrmation if
its design or predictor choices are changed in response to
the new primary test outcomes. New SpuCoMNIST families
would test within-benchmark generalisation. A Waterbirds
procedure with separately ﬁtted development predictors
would test replication of the learning procedure in a second
context, not direct transfer of a frozen SpuCoMNIST predic-
tor. Such direct transfer would require a separate compatible
protocol. Results would remain conditional on two studied
benchmark/model contexts, not arbitrary natural-image de-
ployment.
Development checks should assess the number of failure-
bearing families, eligibility, mixed-outcome settings, mea-
surement validity, inference calibration and computational
cost. Counts of trajectories alone do not establish precision.

B. OPERATIONAL VALUE AS AN EXPLICIT DECISION
TEST
Consider an intended workﬂow in which a team must
reserve specialist audit time or commission a labelled eval-
uation panel before all candidate training runs ﬁnish. An
early risk ranking could inform which candidates receive
those reservations; historical audited runs would supply
the training labels. This is a proposed workﬂow, not a
deployment evaluated here. An early shortlist is useful when
audit slots, specialist time or later data collection must be
reserved before terminal outcomes are available. That is an
operating scenario to validate, not an assumed property of
this inexpensive benchmark. At equal audit count k, deﬁne
a transparent utility scenario
∆U = v [Dlayer(k) − Dbase(k)] − ∆Cm, (9)
where v is an explicitly assumed value per discovered failure
and ∆Cm is incremental monitoring cost. Shared training
and equal-count audit costs cancel under this comparison.
A positive observed discovery difference supplies a possible
beneﬁt region; it does not demonstrate monetary savings
without measured cost and a justiﬁed value assumption. If
exhaustive auditing is cheaper or the baseline reaches the
oracle ceiling, the appropriate conclusion is limited opera-
tional headroom. This keeps scientiﬁc ranking value, early
lead time and practical economics separately assessable.
VIII. CONCLUSION
GradientGuard provides a reproducible framework for ex-
amining early layer-wise connection sensitivity as a signal
for subgroup-audit prioritisation. The completed studies
establish engineering correctness of the intended measure-
ment and identify an encouraging non-slope layer-summary
pattern in a controlled outcome experiment. In the source-
normal held-out pool, L6/L8 improve ranking metrics and
ﬁnd ten failures at twelve inspections compared with eight
for conventional/global predictors, with consistent panel
checks. The original nine-audit comparison remains a tie,
family uncertainty includes zero gain and the added slopes
do not improve primary discovery. The next scientiﬁc op-
portunity is a separately frozen evaluation of the six-feature
representation against stronger structural alternatives and on
a second benchmark context. The present contribution is
exploratory evidence and a reproducible test bed for that
question.
